strengths: Addresses an important and challenging task—fine-grained cross-view localization—with an interpretable local-feature-matching pipeline.
Introduces a practical use of monocular depth priors: lifting only matched ground keypoints to BEV space, avoiding explicit BEV warping and its information loss.
Scale-aware Procrustes alignment enables analytic pose estimation and optional scale recovery, supporting both metric and relative depth models in a plug-and-play manner at inference.

Demonstrates strong results in some challenging settings: 26% lower mean localization error on KITTI cross-area compared with the previous state of the art, and notable improvements under unknown orientation on VIGOR.

Extensive experiments across KITTI and VIGOR, including same-/cross-area, known/unknown orientation, relative depth robustness, qualitative matching, scale recovery, ablations, and runtime/memory reporting.
Qualitative results show semantically meaningful matches (road markings, streetlights, shadows), supporting the claimed interpretability.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is limited: the method builds heavily on prior work (especially FG2) and standard components (DINOv2, SuperGlue-style matching, Procrustes), with no fundamentally new learning module or architecture.

Performance is not consistently state-of-the-art: worse than FG2/HC-Net on KITTI same-area, much worse than FG2 on VIGOR known-orientation, and orientation errors on KITTI are higher than several baselines, so claims of superior localization need stronger qualification.

Evaluation raises potential fairness/leakage concerns: metric depth models used on KITTI may have been trained with KITTI ground-truth depth, while baselines do not necessarily use such depth predictors, making comparisons not fully apples-to-apples.

Training still relies on metric depth for the infoNCE correspondence losses; training with relative depth degrades performance substantially, so the plug-and-play relative-depth claim mainly holds at inference, not training.
Relative-depth inference requires dataset-specific manual choices (initial scale and maximum depth threshold), which limits truly deployment-ready flexibility despite the robustness study.
The similarity-transform assumption and orthorectified aerial imagery assumption may not hold in real datasets, and the paper acknowledges this but does not fully resolve the impact.
Ablations are limited to VIGOR same-area validation, with no cross-dataset ablation or statistical significance testing; code/weights are not mentioned, reducing reproducibility.
Some notation and figure/table presentation could be clearer, e.g., centered point notation is inconsistent in places and the mixed SOTA claims are not tightly scoped.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem: fine-grained cross-view localization with an interpretable local-feature-matching pipeline.

The proposed pose estimation is analytically computed from correspondences via scale-aware Procrustes alignment, which avoids an explicit, lossy ground-to-BEV transformation and can recover scale when using relative depth.

The method supports both metric and relative depth at inference, and experiments show reasonable robustness to arbitrary scale factors and plug-and-play use with different relative depth predictors without finetuning.
On KITTI cross-area localization, it reports a clear improvement over the previous state-of-the-art mean error (7.45 m to 5.51 m).
On VIGOR unknown-orientation evaluation, it achieves strong orientation estimation, with lower mean orientation error than several baselines.
Qualitative results demonstrate semantically meaningful cross-view matches, e.g., road markings, streetlights, and building facades.
Ablations suggest that selecting topmost points is not beneficial and that scale-aware Procrustes alignment is important for performance.
The paper provides useful implementation details, runtime/memory analysis, and discusses limitations and broader impact.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the method largely combines existing components—frozen DINOv2 features, SuperGlue-style dual-softmax matching, monocular depth foundation models, and Umeyama/Procrustes alignment—with modest technical additions over prior work such as FG2.

The experimental results are mixed and do not consistently support the central claim of superior localization. On KITTI same-area, both localization and orientation are substantially worse than prior SOTA (e.g., mean loc 1.11 m vs 0.75 m; orientation R@1° 36.68 vs 61.17). On VIGOR with known orientation, the method is clearly worse than FG2, HC-Net, and others (e.g., same-area mean loc 3.06 m vs FG2 1.95 m).

The scale-recovery claim is not quantitatively evaluated: only qualitative BEV overlays are shown, with no scale-error metric or numerical consistency analysis on benchmarks. The theoretical guarantee requires an exact similarity transform, but aerial images are often not orthorectified and the many-to-one facade/rooftop correspondences violate this assumption.

Practical deployment is overstated: relative depth inference requires manually selected initial scale and maximum depth threshold determined by visual inspection of examples, which is not fully plug-and-play. The method also relies on external metric depth models during training, so the claim of learning from weak pose supervision alone is somewhat misleading.

Ablations are incomplete: only one VIGOR same-area validation setting is considered, with no ablation on KITTI, no sensitivity analysis for number of correspondences, dustbin handling, RANSAC, depth thresholds, or different depth predictors during training.

Baseline comparisons may be unfair or at least not fully contextualized: the method benefits from strong frozen DINOv2 features and additional foundation-model depth priors, while competing methods may not have the same external information or computational budget. Runtime with RANSAC is also quite low (0.42 FPS).

Some methodological details are under-specified, such as how planar BEV coordinates are obtained from lifted 3D points and what assumptions are made about camera roll/pitch; these details matter for reproducibility and correctness.

Orientation estimation on KITTI is much worse than regression-based baselines. The explanation that baselines exploit road-direction priors does not mitigate this practical limitation, especially for autonomous driving or robotics applications.

strengths: The proposed method is simple and interpretable: it avoids explicit ground-to-BEV transformation, directly matches local features between ground and aerial images, and lifts only matched ground keypoints using monocular depth. This reduces information loss and yields explicit correspondences.

Scale-aware Procrustes alignment jointly estimates rotation, translation, and scale, with theoretical support and empirical robustness to arbitrary scaling. The method can use metric depth during training and relative depth at inference without retraining, making it practical with different off-the-shelf depth predictors.

Experimental results are strong in challenging settings: 26% mean localization error reduction on KITTI cross-area, competitive or best results on VIGOR under unknown orientation, and only minor degradation when switching to relative depth models. Qualitative examples and failure-case analysis improve interpretability.

The appendix is thorough, including proofs, additional relative-depth experiments, runtime/memory analysis, limitations, and broader impact. Reproducibility details such as hyperparameters and training setup are mostly provided.
weaknesses: The method is not state-of-the-art in all settings: it is worse than prior work on KITTI same-area, has higher orientation errors on KITTI, and is clearly worse than FG2 on VIGOR when orientation is known. This limits the generality of the claimed superiority.

It relies on a similarity-transform assumption between BEV ground points and aerial points, while real aerial images may not be orthorectified and relative depth models may be scale-shift rather than scale-only invariant. These assumptions are acknowledged but not fully resolved.

The training pipeline uses metric depth predictions and pose-derived infoNCE losses to supervise correspondences, so the claim of learning with only weak pose supervision is somewhat overstated. Training with relative depth is less effective and can degrade unknown-orientation performance.

The ablation study is limited to a few design choices on VIGOR same-area validation. There is no sensitivity analysis for the number of sampled correspondences, sampling strategy, depth model choice during training, RANSAC usage, or backbone variations.
No code or released model is mentioned, and some implementation details (e.g., correspondence sampling procedure) are omitted from the main text, which may hinder reproducibility.

strengths: The proposed Loc² method provides a clean and interpretable formulation for cross-view localization that directly matches ground-aerial local features and lifts them to BEV using monocular depth, then estimates pose via scale-aware Procrustes alignment. This avoids BEV warping distortions that prior methods suffer from, which is a well-motivated design choice.
The method is weakly supervised, requiring only 3-DoF camera poses rather than pixel-level ground-aerial correspondences, which is a practical and important property for real-world deployment.

The paper demonstrates strong and consistent state-of-the-art performance in the challenging unknown-orientation setting on both KITTI and VIGOR, which is arguably the hardest and most practically relevant evaluation scenario.

The scale-aware Procrustes formulation is technically sound, differentiably integrated into the pipeline, and elegantly supports both metric and relative depth inputs. The proof in the appendix is complete and correct, and the scale-invariance experiments (Fig. 12, Table 15) convincingly demonstrate robustness to arbitrary scale factors.

The interpretability contributions are substantive: correspondence-based outlier detection via RANSAC, strong correlation between inlier ratio and pose error (Fig. 4), and visual layout-overlay alignment (Fig. 5, 13) that enables identifying erroneous ground-truth as well as localization failures.

The evaluation is thorough, covering KITTI and VIGOR with both same-area and cross-area splits, known and unknown orientations, multiple depth predictors (UniK3D, BiFuse++, UniFuse), and extensive ablations on hyperparameters, BEV-plane matching, and homography-based pose estimation (Tables 4-14).
The paper includes a reproducibility statement, an LLM usage statement, runtime and memory comparisons (Table 16), and detailed implementation details, which aids reproducibility.
The qualitative results (Fig. 3, 8, 9, 10, 11) illustrate semantic correspondence behavior, including matching building facades, road markings, and trees, and honestly discuss failure cases.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is essentially a composition of existing components (frozen DINOv2 features, off-the-shelf monocular depth predictors, standard dual-softmax matching, and classical Procrustes alignment). The novelty is moderate, and the paper does not introduce a fundamentally new learning mechanism or representation.

The reported results are mixed: on KITTI same-area ±10° and on VIGOR known-orientation settings, the method is outperformed by baselines such as FG² (e.g., 1.13 m vs 0.75 m on KITTI same-area ±10°; 3.43 m vs 2.41 m on VIGOR cross-area known orientation). The paper acknowledges this but the overall gain is concentrated in the unknown-orientation setting.

The method relies on external depth predictors (UniK3D, BiFuse++, UniFuse) whose quality directly affects performance, and the memory footprint of the metric-depth variant is substantial (2.1 GB with UniK3D). This dependency is not fully analyzed—there is no study of how depth predictor errors propagate to localization errors.

The interpretability claims are mostly qualitative and visual. While Fig. 4 shows a correlation between inlier ratio and pose error, there is no quantitative metric or benchmark that measures interpretability, making the advantage somewhat subjective.

The cross-dataset generalization experiment on CVACT (Sec. 4.5) is evaluated only qualitatively via visual overlays, without any quantitative localization or orientation errors, since CVACT lacks precise labels. This limits the strength of the generalization claim.

The paper does not discuss failure modes tied to depth estimation explicitly—e.g., regions with poor depth prediction (sky, reflective surfaces, textureless areas)—which is a practical concern given the reliance on monocular depth.

The claim of 'state-of-the-art accuracy' is somewhat selective, since the method is only SOTA in the unknown-orientation regime and not in known-orientation, which is a common operational setting; the paper should better frame this trade-off as a design choice rather than a general SOTA claim.

strengths: The paper presents a clean and interpretable cross-view localization pipeline that establishes local feature correspondences directly between ground and aerial images, avoiding the ray-directional distortions and information loss of BEV-warping approaches.

The scale-aware Procrustes alignment is a principled and differentiable formulation that allows the method to handle both metric and relative depth at inference, and empirically the method is shown to be robust to arbitrary scale factors (Fig. 12) and to different relative-depth predictors (BiFuse++, UniFuse).

Strong empirical results in the most challenging setting: on VIGOR cross-area with unknown orientation, Loc² substantially improves localization (4.23 m vs. 5.41 m for CCVPE and 10.02 m for FG²) and orientation (11.67° vs. 27.78° / 31.41°), and on KITTI cross-area it also achieves the best mean/median localization error.

The paper includes an extensive experimental section: two datasets with same-area/cross-area splits, known/unknown orientation, cross-dataset generalization to CVACT, interpretability analyses (inlier ratio vs. error, layout overlay), and a thorough ablation study (Sec. 4.6 and Appendix A) covering coordinate assignment, scale-awareness, matching/pose-estimation variants, temperature, depth thresholds, etc.

The interpretability claims are backed by concrete evidence: correspondence quality correlates with localization accuracy, and the re-scaled ground-layout overlay provides a visual cue for identifying failures (e.g., Fig. 5(c) exposes a ground-truth error).
Reproducibility is well supported: hyperparameters and training details are fully specified, runtime/memory comparisons are reported, and code release is promised.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental relative to FG² (Xia & Alahi, 2025). The core components—dual-softmax local feature matching with a frozen DINOv2 backbone, depth-lifting of matched points, and Procrustes-based pose estimation—are all standard, and the main changes (matching in the image plane rather than BEV, and replacing orthogonal with scale-aware Procrustes) are natural extensions rather than a fundamentally new formulation.

The 'state-of-the-art' claim is only partially supported. On KITTI (Table 1), Loc² is worse than FG² on same-area and worse than CCVPE/SliceMatch on orientation under both ±10° and ±180° noise; on VIGOR known orientation (Table 2) it is worse than FG². The abstract and introduction overstate the generality of the SOTA claim.

Training depends on off-the-shelf metric-depth models (Unik3D, DepthAnythingV2), and the reported gains are entangled with the quality of these frozen depth predictions. The paper does not sufficiently disentangle the contribution of the matching module from the depth backbone, e.g., by controlling for depth quality.

The scale-aware Procrustes derivation in Sec. 3.2 (Eq. 5) essentially shows that in the idealized, noise-free case s* = s. This is a consistency argument rather than a robustness result; it does not demonstrate why the estimator recovers the correct scale under realistic correspondence noise and depth errors, which is the practically relevant regime.

Some claims are asserted rather than demonstrated. For instance, the statement that 'our local feature matching becomes end-to-end trainable using only camera pose supervision' glosses over the fact that correspondence supervision via the infoNCE losses relies on ground-truth pose to compute pseudo-correspondences, and that metric depth is required during training.

The failure of the method to exploit the road-facing prior on KITTI is acknowledged but not addressed; this limits practical applicability where such a prior is informative and where orientation accuracy matters (e.g., autonomous driving).

Positioning against FG², the paper's closest competitor, is somewhat thin: FG² is dismissed mainly on grounds of BEV-matching inefficiency, but the empirical gap on known-orientation VIGOR (where FG² is better) is not analyzed in depth.

strengths: Presents a novel and well-motivated formulation for fine-grained cross-view localization: matching local features directly in the image plane and lifting matched ground points to BEV via monocular depth, avoiding the ray-direction distortions and height information loss of prior BEV-based matching approaches.

Introduces a differentiable scale-aware Procrustes alignment that jointly estimates 3-DoF pose and depth scale, enabling end-to-end training with only camera pose supervision and supporting both metric and relative depth predictors at inference.

Demonstrates strong empirical performance on KITTI and VIGOR, especially in challenging cross-area and unknown-orientation settings, with clear improvements over recent methods such as FG2, CCVPE, SliceMatch, and DenseFlow on localization metrics.

Provides extensive ablations and analyses, including top-points vs. all points, scale-aware vs. scale-ignoring alignment, image-plane vs. BEV-plane matching, homography-based pose estimation, RANSAC, depth thresholds, resolution, and hyperparameters, which convincingly support the main design choices.

Offers practical interpretability: visualized correspondences and ground-layout overlay give intuitive cues about localization quality, and the inlier ratio correlates with pose error, enabling RANSAC-based outlier detection.
Shows robustness to different depth predictors and arbitrary scale factors, making the method more practical for real-world deployment where only relative depth may be available.
Reproducibility is well supported: clear implementation details, hyperparameters, runtime/memory analysis, theoretical proof in the appendix, and a commitment to release code.
The paper is clearly written and well organized, with informative figures and a coherent presentation of method, experiments, and limitations.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental relative to recent work such as FG2: the core idea of local feature matching across ground and aerial views has already been established, and the main algorithmic changes are matching in the image plane and using scale-aware Procrustes alignment.

Orientation estimation is not consistently state-of-the-art: on KITTI, orientation errors are worse than FG2 and HC-Net in several settings, even though orientation is part of the claimed 3-DoF pose estimation.

The method depends on off-the-shelf monocular depth estimators and does not fine-tune or train depth, so performance is limited by the quality of these frozen models; failure cases in dense vegetation, water, and occlusion remain.
Interpretability claims are largely qualitative; no quantitative metric or user study is provided to substantiate that correspondence quality reliably reflects localization accuracy.
RANSAC-based inference is slow (0.42 FPS with RANSAC), while omitting RANSAC reduces accuracy; the practical speed-accuracy trade-off could be better characterized.
Cross-dataset generalization on CVACT is only qualitative due to the lack of labels, limiting the strength of that evaluation.
Potential ethical/privacy implications of fine-grained cross-view localization are not discussed, which is a minor but relevant omission for a deployable localization system.
